unit.title: Reflect on and improve own professional practice

summary: This unit teaches you to look honestly at your own work and make it better: how to reflect using a reflective cycle and a journal, how to measure your work against standards and the limits of your role, how to ask for and use feedback, how to find your strengths and weaknesses with self-assessment and a SWOT, how to set SMART goals and write a development plan, how to keep learning in Jamaica, how to keep a portfolio and protect client privacy, and how to look after your own wellbeing.

blocks.p: Qualified therapists, stylists and technicians do not stop learning on the day they finish their training. Skills change, products change and clients change. The therapists who do best are not always the most talented. They are the ones who **look at their own work honestly, learn from it and keep improving**. This unit teaches you how. It is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees, and the methods work in any trade.

Reflecting on your practice is not about blaming yourself. It is a habit of asking, 'What happened, why, and what will I do next time?' A therapist who does this gets better results, has happier clients and works more safely.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the salon
rows: Say what reflection is and why it matters
Use a reflective cycle and keep a reflective journal
Work to standards and within your limits
Compare your work with unit standards, salon procedures and your job description
Know your scope of practice and refer when a treatment is beyond it
Ask clients, supervisors and co-workers for feedback
Respond calmly and act on what you hear
Find your strengths and areas to improve
Be honest about weaknesses and proud of strengths
Set goals and make a development plan
Write and review a personal development plan
Courses, supplier training, trade shows, shadowing, mentoring and online learning
Keep a portfolio and training record
Protect client privacy in your records and photographs
Look after your wellbeing and behave professionally

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks done in a group: giving a short hand and arm massage, collecting feedback and writing a reflective account with a SMART goal; then writing a SWOT and a personal development plan and making a group poster on ways to keep learning. The assessor reads your accounts as well as watching your work.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Your reflections are for you. Honest writing helps you most. Do not write down a client's name or private details. Leave private matters such as your own health out of anything you share.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Reflective practice and the reflective cycle

blocks.p: To **reflect** on your practice is to think carefully about your own work in order to learn from it and improve. You look back at what happened, how you felt, what went well and what did not, and then decide what to change.

head: Without reflection
With reflection
rows: A mistake is understood and not repeated
You know why something went well, and can repeat it
A complaint comes as a surprise
You notice a problem early and fix it
You grow in skill and confidence

ul: Reflect **soon after** the treatment, while it is fresh in your mind.
Ask yourself: **What went well? What could I do better?**
Reflection leads to **action**. Thinking without changing anything is not enough.
Good reflection looks at your feelings too: nerves or stress can change how well you work.

blocks.p: A **reflective cycle** is a set of steps that guide you from what happened to what you will do next. A well-known one was written by Graham Gibbs and has six stages.

head: Stage
The question
What you write
rows: The facts, in order: who, what, when, where. No opinions yet.
What was I thinking and feeling?
Your feelings before, during and after, and how they affected the work.
What was good and what was bad about it?
What went well and what did not.
The causes: what you did, what others did, and what else was going on.
What else could I have done?
What will I do next time?
Clear changes, with dates, and how you will check them.

blocks.p: Another common model, by David Kolb, has four stages: **have an experience**, **reflect on it**, **draw conclusions**, and **try the new way**. Simple models are alike: describe, think it through, plan, and act. Then you do it again with the new plan.
Trainee Nadine gave a leg wax in the Centre's salon. It took 70 minutes instead of 45, a few hairs were missed, and the client's skin was quite red at the end.

head: Stage
Nadine's reflection
rows: I waxed both legs for a client booked for 45 minutes. It took 70 minutes. Some hairs were left on the shins and her skin was red by the end.
I was nervous and rushed because the assessor was watching. I pressed hard when I pulled the strips, and I felt embarrassed when I saw the redness.
Good: I checked for contraindications and she signed the card. Not good: the time, the missed hairs and the red skin.

I did not set out strips and wax before she arrived, so I kept stopping. I applied wax in patches that were too big. I pulled the strip in the wrong direction and too slowly, which pulled the skin. I did not check the wax temperature again halfway through.
I need to set up properly, use smaller patches, pull parallel to the skin and quickly, and keep checking the temperature.

(1) Set up everything before each client from now on. (2) Practise small patches on two classmates this week. (3) Ask my instructor to watch my strip technique on Friday. (4) Time myself and review in two weeks.

blocks.note: Notice how Nadine's plan contains actions she can check, with dates. A plan that says only 'be better next time' cannot be checked.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **reflective journal** (or log) is a record of your work, your thoughts and the lessons you have learned. Keep it regularly, even if only a few lines.

ul: Date each entry and say what the treatment or task was.
Use a cycle so that you do not just describe. Always include what you will do differently.
Be honest. The journal is for learning, not for showing off.
Do not write client names or private details. Use a code such as 'Client A' or the date and treatment.
Read old entries from time to time to see how you have improved and what keeps repeating.
Keep the journal safe, and share it only with your instructor or supervisor if you choose.
Write in the first person: 'I did ...', 'I felt ...'.
Give reasons: 'I did this because ...'.
Include something you did well, as well as something to improve.
End with an action plan that has at least one SMART goal.

blocks.p: You cannot judge your own work unless you know the standard it should meet. In a salon there are several standards, each with a different purpose.

head: Standard
What it tells you
rows: What a competent worker must be able to do in each unit; the basis of your assessment.
The step-by-step written method the salon expects every therapist to follow for a treatment.
What your employer expects you to do in your job.
Rules on how staff should behave at work: honesty, respect, confidentiality, dress, timekeeping.
How to use products and equipment safely.
The law and health and safety rules
What you must do by law, including client privacy.

ul: Compare your work with these standards. For example: 'The unit says I must complete a record card; do mine always have a signature?'
**Self-assessment** is rating your own skills against a checklist, such as the unit's list of tasks.

blocks.p: Your **scope of practice** is the limit of what you are trained, qualified and allowed to do. It is set by your training, your qualifications, your employer's rules and the law.

ul: A treatment you have not been trained in is **outside your scope**. Say honestly that you are not trained and refer the client to someone who is.
You do not diagnose illness or treat medical conditions. You refer the client to a doctor.
Do not use a technique you have only seen in a video or heard about. Get proper training and be assessed first.

If you make a mistake or miss a step, such as leaving out a skin test the maker requires, **report it honestly**, check that the client is safe, reflect on why it happened and change your routine. Hiding a mistake is a worse fault than the mistake.

head: Quality
What it looks like
rows: Arrives on time for work and appointments; starts and finishes treatments on time
Gives true prices and true information; admits mistakes; never makes false claims
Does what she says she will do; completes records and tasks
Treats clients and colleagues politely; respects different backgrounds and beliefs
Clean uniform, clean hands, clean station
Takes feedback well; asks questions; keeps learning

blocks.p: You cannot see everything about your own work. Other people see things you miss. **Feedback** is information from others about how you are doing. The more sources you use, the clearer the picture.

head: Source
How you get it
What it tells you
rows: A short feedback form filled in privately
Comments during and after the treatment
Whether she rebooks or recommends you
How the service felt: comfort, time, results, manner.
Whether your work meets the salon's standard.
Things you do not notice yourself.
How you compare with the unit standard.
Photos of your work compared with the standard

ul: A **client feedback form** should be short, easy and private. A client may not say something negative to your face, but she may write it down.
An **appraisal** is a regular meeting where a supervisor and a therapist review her work and set goals for the next period.
**Client retention**, keeping clients coming back, is a sign of good service. If most clients do not rebook, ask why.

blocks.p: **Constructive feedback** is fair and helps you improve: it says what was good, what could be better and how. 'Your pressure was a bit light; try a little more on the shoulders' is constructive. 'You are bad at massage' is not.

flow: Do not make excuses or argue
Reflect on it later, when you are calm
Plan changes and tell the person what you will do
Check later that you have improved

ul: Praise is feedback too. Note what you do well and keep doing it.
Feedback such as 'lovely, but a bit rushed' contains two messages. Accept the compliment and treat the criticism as useful.
One comment may be a personal opinion, but if several people say the same thing, take it seriously.
If feedback seems unfair, ask for an example and reflect on it with your supervisor, rather than dismiss it.
A complaint is feedback that the client felt strongly about. Stay calm, listen, apologise for how she feels, and tell your supervisor.
Do not argue or blame the client or another worker.
Record what happened, and reflect on what you can learn.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, clients often tell friends and family about a service, and messages and photos spread quickly on social media. One unhappy client can cost you many others, and one happy client can bring you many. Take feedback seriously, and thank clients who give it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use a list of the skills your job needs and rate yourself on each one, for example 1 (needs a lot of work) to 4 (very confident). Back each rating with an example or with feedback. For a beauty therapist the list could include: consultation, hygiene, treatment skills, time management, communication, record keeping, product knowledge and customer care.

head: Skill
My rating (1 to 4)
Evidence
Next step
rows: Supervisor said my questions were thorough
Three treatments over time last month
Set up before clients arrive; time each step
Check every card before the client leaves
Client feedback: 'lovely'; one said 'a bit light'
Ask about pressure at the start and during

blocks.p: A **SWOT analysis** helps you to see your position clearly. SWOT stands for **Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats**. Strengths and weaknesses are things **inside you**; opportunities and threats are things **outside you**.

head: Where
Helpful
Harmful
rows: **Threats**: things that could harm your progress

head: Part
Examples for a trainee beauty therapist
rows: Slow at writing up client records
Poor at estimating how long a treatment takes
A free supplier training day next month
A mentor offered by a senior therapist
The Centre offering the next level
Customers cutting spending when prices rise
A busy family life that leaves little time to study

ul: Be honest. A SWOT with only strengths, or only weaknesses, is not useful.
Write at least two points in each box.
A weakness is not a failure. Naming it is the first step to fixing it.
Note your strengths too, so that you can build on them and feel confident.
Use the SWOT to set goals: build on strengths, fix weaknesses, use opportunities and plan for threats.

blocks.p: A vague wish, such as 'get better at facials', is hard to achieve, because you cannot tell when you have succeeded. A **SMART goal** is clear.

head: Letter
Meaning
Question to ask
rows: What exactly do I want to achieve?
How will I know I have done it?
Can I really do it with my time, money and support?
Does it matter for my work and my plan?

head: Weak goal
SMART goal
rows: By the end of March, carry out 10 supervised leg waxes in under 45 minutes each, with no red or broken skin, checked by my supervisor
Complete the supplier's one-day skin care product course on 15 February and explain the range to three clients by 28 February
From Monday, check every record card for a signature before the client leaves; my supervisor audits ten cards at the end of the month and all are complete

ul: A **deadline** helps you plan and check your progress.
Two or three goals at a time are enough. Too many goals mean none is done.

blocks.p: A **personal development plan** is a written plan of what you will learn, how you will learn it and by when. It starts from your reflection, your feedback and your SWOT.

head: Goal (SMART)
Actions
Help or resources
Cost (JMD)
Target date
Progress
rows: Carry out 10 supervised leg waxes in under 45 minutes each
Ask the instructor to watch my strip technique
Complete the supplier's skin care course
Supplier training day; supervisor lets me swap a shift
Often free or low cost; ask

ul: Agree it with your supervisor so that they can support you.
Write down your progress and keep evidence: certificates, feedback, dated photos of your work.
**Review** it regularly, for example every few months, and update it. Goals that have been met are replaced; goals that have not need a new plan.
Share one or two goals with a colleague. People who tell someone are more likely to keep going.

blocks.p: **Continuing professional development (CPD)** is learning that you keep doing throughout your career. In beauty therapy it is essential: new products, new methods and new safety advice appear all the time.

head: Way to learn
What it is
Good for
Check
rows: NVQ-J units or the next level; short courses at the Centre or other providers
Recognised skills and a pathway to progress
Is the provider recognised, for example by NCTVET or working with HEART/NSTA Trust? What are the fees?
A product maker or distributor shows you how to use new products or equipment
Is it about the supplier's own products only? Is it free?
Events where suppliers show new products and techniques
Seeing new trends and meeting suppliers
Treat product claims with care; check before using anything new on clients
Watching a skilled therapist at work
Seeing real practice and good habits
Ask permission and respect client privacy
An experienced person gives advice, support and honest guidance
Choose someone who is respected and willing
Practising with feedback from a senior
Be clear what you are and are not allowed to do alone
Books, trade magazines, websites, videos and online courses
Studying at home in your own time
Check that the source is reliable and the method is safe; do not use a technique on clients until you have been trained

blocks.h: Choosing a reliable course or source

ul: Does it match **your goals** from the development plan?
Is the provider **recognised**, and is the qualification accepted by employers and NCTVET or HEART/NSTA Trust?
Is it **safe**? Does it teach correct safety, hygiene and consultation?
Is it **good value**? Compare the cost in JMD, the time it takes and what you get. Be wary of 'become an expert in a weekend' promises.
Ask other therapists and your instructor what they know of it.

blocks.p: A Level 2 beauty therapist who wants to progress can ask her training centre or HEART/NSTA Trust about further qualifications, such as NVQ-J units or the next level. Her portfolio and training record show what she has already done. Further learning may lead to promotion, a wider range of treatments, supervision or running her own business.

blocks.note: Never use a new treatment or product on a client because you read about it or saw it online. Check that it is safe, get proper training and be assessed first. A client trusts you with her skin and her health.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Many Jamaican therapists work from home or run small businesses. Even if you work alone, you still need feedback, and a mentor or a group of other therapists can give it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **portfolio** is a collection of evidence of your skills and development. It shows employers and assessors what you can do and how you have improved.

head: Keep in your portfolio
Why
rows: Your development plans and SWOT sheets
Show you learn from your work
Certificates and a training record: the courses you have done with their dates
Show the effect of your work
Show progress; they must be taken with permission

ul: Date and label every item. Update the portfolio regularly.
Keep **copies** of certificates: originals can be lost.
Use it in interviews and at appraisals to show progress over time.
The best evidence of improvement is a set of **dated records, feedback and photos** from different times.

blocks.p: Your reflections and portfolio come from real clients, and their private information must be protected. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act, a person's personal information must be kept private and secure.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Use codes such as 'Client A' in your journal
Write full names, phone numbers or health details
Ask the client's permission before taking a photo of her, and show only the area you worked on
Photograph her face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it
Keep records in a locked drawer or a password-protected file
Leave records on a desk or in an open chat group
Ask before showing or posting a photo anywhere
Post photos of clients, or stories about them, on social media without consent
Share only with people who need it, such as your supervisor
Talk about a client in front of other clients or friends

blocks.note: A photo of a client's hands may seem harmless, but it can still identify her by a ring, a tattoo or a distinctive nail design. Ask first, every time.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Looking after yourself: wellbeing and ergonomics

blocks.p: Beauty therapy is physical, social and emotional work. You stand for hours, bend, hold awkward positions, handle products, and give your attention and care to many people. If you do not look after yourself, your health, your work and your clients suffer.

head: Demand
What can go wrong
What you can do
rows: Set the couch, stool or chair at the right height
Keep your back straight, feet apart, knees soft
Use body weight instead of thumb strength
Drink water; eat regularly; use fans or air conditioning sensibly

blocks.p: **Ergonomics** is arranging your work, such as the couch height, the trolley and the stool, so that it fits your body and prevents strain and injury. If you often have back pain after treatments, look at your posture and the couch height when you reflect.

ul: Long days, demanding clients, money worries and family needs can cause stress. Stress can harm your health and your work.
**Resilience** is the ability to cope with setbacks and stress and keep going.
Plan your week, set up before clients arrive, and leave time between appointments.
Sleep, eat, drink water and rest. Take real breaks.
Talk to your supervisor, a mentor or a trusted friend about problems. Asking for help is a sign of strength.
If you feel unwell for a long time, see a doctor.
A tired, stressed therapist is more likely to make mistakes, be late, or be short with a client.
Being **punctual** is part of being professional: it shows respect for the client and the team.
Include your wellbeing in your reflection: 'Was I too tired? Was my posture poor? What can I change?'

blocks.note: In practical work, a therapist who is unwell with a fever, a sore throat or an infection should not work on clients that day. Tell your supervisor. Working while infectious puts clients at risk.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: I can explain what reflective practice is and why it matters.
I can use a reflective cycle, and say what each stage asks.
I can keep a reflective journal that protects client privacy.
I can name the standards I should compare my work with.
I can explain scope of practice and what to do when a treatment is beyond it.
I can report a mistake honestly and change my routine.
I can collect feedback from clients, a supervisor and peers.
I can respond to feedback calmly and act on it.
I can carry out a self-assessment and a SWOT with examples in each box.
I can write a SMART goal and explain each letter.
I can write a personal development plan and say how to use and review it.
I can describe ways to keep learning in Jamaica and choose reliable ones.
I can keep a portfolio and a training record.
I can take and use photographs only with consent and protect client information.
I can look after my posture, wellbeing and stress, and act professionally.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each point, not only the point. For example: 'I leave the client's name out of my journal, because her information is private and the journal might be read by someone else.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Thinking about your own work to learn and improve.
A set of steps that guide you from what happened to what you will do next.
A record of your work, thoughts and lessons learned.
Rating your own skills against a checklist.
Information from others about how you are doing.
Fair comments that help you improve.
A regular meeting to review work and set goals.
The document saying what a competent worker must be able to do in a unit.
The step-by-step written method the salon expects for a treatment.
Rules on how staff should behave at work.
The limits of what you are trained, qualified and allowed to do.
A written plan of what you will learn, how and by when.
Learning that you keep doing through your career.
Watching a skilled therapist work, to learn.
An experienced person who gives advice and support.
An event where suppliers show new products and techniques.
A collection of evidence of your skills and development.
A written list of courses done, with dates.
Arranging work so that it fits the body and prevents strain.
The ability to cope with setbacks and stress and keep going.

c1.title: A leg wax that went wrong in Spanish Town
c1.text: Trainee Camille gave a leg wax in a salon in Spanish Town. It ran 25 minutes over the booked time, a few hairs were left, and the client's skin was red. That evening Camille writes in her journal: 'It went badly. The client was difficult. I will try harder.' She includes the client's full name and phone number so that she remembers who it was.

c2.title: A feedback card in St. Ann's Bay
c2.text: At a salon in St. Ann's Bay, a client fills in a feedback form privately after a facial. She ticks 'very good' for results and 'excellent' for cleanliness, but writes: 'The therapist was lovely, but she kept looking at her phone and didn't explain what she was doing.' The therapist, Sasha, feels hurt and says to her colleague, 'Some people are never pleased.'

c3.title: A plan for the year in Lucea
c3.text: Roshane, a Level 2 therapist in Lucea, writes a SWOT. Her entries include: 'I am good at nail art', 'I find it hard to speak up when I disagree with a client', 'A new supplier is opening a training centre in town next month', and 'Another salon opened across the road'. She then writes this goal: 'Get better at confidence.'

c4.title: Choosing a course in Christiana
c4.text: Marvin, a therapist in Christiana, has JMD 45,000 saved for training. He is offered two choices. One is an online course that promises 'master every treatment in three days' from a company he has not heard of. The other is a recognised short course at a training centre that works with HEART/NSTA Trust, with a certificate and a practical assessment, and costs JMD 38,000. His goal is to give safe, well-made gel nails.

c5.title: A journal and a chat group in Montego Bay
c5.text: Trainee Shanice in Montego Bay keeps a notebook of her practice. She writes the full name of each client, their health problems and photographs of their faces and hands. She also posts the photos in a large phone chat group of trainees and friends with captions about the clients' skin. A classmate says she should stop; Shanice says the photos are 'only for learning'.

c6.title: A tired therapist in Mandeville
c6.text: Candice works six days a week at a salon in Mandeville. She often arrives 15 minutes late because of her bus, skips lunch to catch up, and has had back pain for months. Last week she snapped at a client who asked a question, and she has made two small errors on record cards. When she reflected, she wrote down that she was 'just tired'.

questions.q: What is the main weakness in Camille's journal entry?
o: It gives too much detail about how the leg wax was done
It blames the client and has no analysis or plan for change
It was written on the same day, when it should wait a month
It is too short and so cannot be kept in her portfolio
questions.why: A useful reflection describes what happened, gives reasons and ends with a plan. 'I will try harder' cannot be checked, and blaming the client avoids learning.

questions.q: Camille wants to find out why the wax ran 25 minutes over. In a reflective cycle, which stage is this?
o: Description
Action plan
Analysis
Conclusion
questions.why: Analysis asks why things happened and looks at causes. Description gives the facts, conclusion says what has been learned, and the action plan says what to do next.

questions.q: What is wrong with the client's name and phone number in the journal?
o: A journal can be read by others, so private details are left out
Names make a journal look unprofessional to a supervisor
The name is fine, but the phone number should be kept secret
Clients' names are needed so that the journal counts as evidence
questions.why: A client's personal information is private. Use a code such as 'Client A', and keep contact details on the record card, which is locked away.

questions.q: Which action plan is best for Camille?
o: Try hard to do better next time, and stay calm through the whole service
Book more clients each day so that she gets faster through practice
Set up before each client, and ask for her strip technique to be observed
Avoid leg waxes until she feels fully ready to do them
questions.why: A good plan has specific actions, dates and a way to check. Doing more clients without a method repeats the mistake; avoiding the treatment does not build the skill.

questions.q: How should Sasha treat the client's comment?
o: As useful feedback: she should reflect on it and act
As unfair, since the client ticked good boxes for the rest
As a complaint to be argued with at the next visit
As something to keep from her supervisor
questions.why: The comment is specific and helpful: using a phone and not explaining the steps are things she can change. Feedback is a gift when it points to something fixable.

questions.q: Which response would be best for Sasha to give her colleague?
o: That the client is wrong, as she gave good marks for the results
That she will stop reading the forms and trust her own opinion
That the client does not understand how a facial is done
That the comment is fair, and she will explain each step
questions.why: Responding to feedback means listening, not making excuses, and deciding on changes. Dismissing it loses the chance to improve.

questions.q: Why is a private feedback form a good way to collect feedback?
o: It means the therapist never has to hear a criticism herself
Clients may write what they would not say face to face
The law requires a signed feedback form for each treatment
It lets the salon decide which clients to keep coming
questions.why: Many clients do not like to criticise a therapist to her face. A short private form lets them be honest, and gives the therapist information she can use.

questions.q: Where does 'Another salon opened across the road' go in Roshane's SWOT?
o: Strengths
Weaknesses
Opportunities
Threats
questions.why: It is outside her and could harm her business, so it is a threat. Strengths and weaknesses are inside her; opportunities and threats are outside.

questions.q: Where does 'I find it hard to speak up when I disagree with a client' go?
o: Weaknesses
Strengths
Opportunities
Threats
questions.why: It is something inside her that she could improve, so it is a weakness. Naming it is the first step to a goal such as practising explaining contraindications.

questions.q: Why is 'Get better at confidence' not a good goal?
o: It is not relevant, because confidence does not affect her work
It is too easy to achieve, so it would not help her to grow
It has no clear action, measure or deadline to check against
It cannot be achieved in a year, however hard she works
questions.why: A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. 'Get better at confidence' is a wish, not a plan.

questions.q: Which opportunity should Roshane build into her development plan?
o: Waiting for the salon across the road to close down so her work grows
Taking on more clients, whatever it does to her time for study
Staying away from all training until she feels more confident
Booking the supplier's training next month, if it fits her goal
questions.why: An opportunity is a chance to use. A training day that matches a goal can be turned into a SMART action with a date, a cost and a way to check.

questions.q: Which course best suits Marvin's goal of safe, well-made gel nails?
o: The recognised course, which includes a practical assessment
The online course that promises to teach every treatment in three days
Whichever course costs less, to keep money in reserve
Neither, since a working therapist needs no more training
questions.why: A recognised course with a practical assessment teaches safe method and gives a certificate employers accept. 'Master everything in three days' promises are a warning sign.

questions.q: What should Marvin check about the online company?
o: Whether its website looks modern and shows happy students
Whether it is recognised, safe and good value for money
How many followers the company has on social media
Whether the course is shorter than any other on offer
questions.why: Reliable training is recognised, safe and good value. Ask other therapists and your instructor.

questions.q: After he learns the new method, what should Marvin do before using it on clients?
o: Try it on clients straight away, so that he gets used to it quickly
Wait a full year before using it on any client, however good the course
Practise under supervision until he is assessed as safe
Post a video of himself using it to get opinions
questions.why: A therapist must be trained and competent in a technique before offering it. Supervised practice and assessment protect clients.

questions.q: What is the main fault in Shanice's notebook and photos?
o: She keeps her notes in a paper notebook, not on a computer
She writes about each client at too great a length
She keeps photos of her work for her own learning
Names, health details and faces are kept without any privacy
questions.why: Clients' names, health information and faces are private. Use codes, take photos only with consent, and show only the work area.

questions.q: Why is posting the photos in the chat group wrong even if it is 'only for learning'?
o: The clients did not agree, and they could be identified
Only photos of faces break the rules, not photos of hands
Chat groups are allowed if every member is a trainee
Photos are fine as long as the captions give no names
questions.why: Learning does not give you the right to share a client's image or details. Without her permission it breaks her privacy and the trust the profession depends on.

questions.q: What should Shanice do now?
o: Cover the faces in the group photos and keep the captions
Remove the photos, tell her instructor and change how she records
Ask the classmates in the group to keep the photos secret
Do nothing more, since only friends and trainees can see them
questions.why: Put it right as far as she can, be honest with her instructor, and change her routine: codes in the journal, consent for photos, and no sharing in chat groups.

questions.q: What is the most likely link between Candice's tiredness and her record card errors and snapping at a client?
o: Clients in Mandeville are more demanding than clients elsewhere
Record cards are too complicated for a salon that is this busy
Tiredness and stress make people careless and short-tempered
She was never trained to speak politely to clients at all
questions.why: Tiredness and stress make people careless and short-tempered. Wellbeing and professional standards go together, so include your own health when you reflect.

questions.q: What could Candice do about her back pain?
o: Work longer hours so that her muscles get used to the strain
Stop doing treatments for a month, then start again as before
Take painkillers every day and carry on working as before
Check her posture and couch height, and see a doctor if it goes on
questions.why: Back pain after treatments often comes from posture and equipment height. Ergonomics, breaks and stretching help, and a doctor should check pain that continues.

questions.q: What would be the best SMART goal for her lateness?
o: From Monday, catch the earlier bus and arrive before opening
Try harder not to be late, and say sorry to the team
Never be late again for as long as she works at the salon
Change to a job closer to home as soon as one is offered to her
questions.why: A SMART goal is clear, measurable and time-bound, with a way to check. 'Try not to be late' cannot be measured.
